entity_types.definition: A mention that refers to an individual human being (real or fictional) by name: given name, surname, full name, mononym, or romanization/transliteration of such a name.
includes: initials used as part of a name
excludes: places and products named after people
usernames/handles (not evaluated in this taxonomy version)
names of animals, pets, vehicles and other non-human referents

language_profiles.name: English
conventions: Titles and honorifics (Dr., Mr., Ms., Prof., Sir, Judge) are excluded from the PERSON span.
A possessive 's is excluded from the PERSON span.
Generational suffixes (Jr., Sr., III) are included in the PERSON span.
Initials and their periods are included when they are part of the name.
Surrounding punctuation and quotation marks are excluded.
Eponymous terms (Ohm's law, Parkinson's disease, Nobel Prize) are not PERSON mentions; the whole term is a not-person span.
Plural or collective references to families or namesakes (the Joneses, two Johns) have no convention in taxonomy 0.1.0; cases using them are marked 'either' and recorded as a known gap.
Post-nominal degrees and honours (PhD, MD, OBE) and titles written without a period (Ms) are excluded from the PERSON span, like prefixed titles.

language_profiles.name: Korean
conventions: Josa (particles such as 은/는/이/가/을/를/에게/한테/께서/의/와/과/도/만) are excluded from the PERSON span.
Honorific suffixes and titles (씨, 님, 선생님, 교수님, 부장, 대표) are excluded from the PERSON span.
A vocative or informal suffix (야/아, 이 after a consonant-final given name) is excluded from the PERSON span.
A surname alone (e.g. 김 씨) is a PERSON mention when it refers to a person; the following 씨 is excluded.
Romanized names are one PERSON span including internal hyphens (Kim Min-su).
A name followed by a parenthesized alternate-script form yields two PERSON spans, one per form.
Spacing inside a name (김 민수) does not change the span: the whole spaced name is one span.

span_conventions.offset_unit: Unicode code points over NFC-normalized text; fixtures additionally carry UTF-8 byte and UTF-16 code unit offsets.
span_conventions.overlap: Expectation spans in one case never overlap.
span_conventions.whitespace: Spans never begin or end with whitespace.

expectation_kinds.definition: The span is a PERSON mention in this context. A PERSON prediction that matches the span is correct.
The span looks name-like but is not a PERSON mention in this context. No PERSON prediction should overlap it.
Both readings are defensible given only this text. The case is an honest ambiguity; consumers must not score it as a hard positive or hard negative.

evidence_classes.definition: Derived from an imported corpus with a registered source record.
Expectation justified by a cited linguistic or naming reference.
An external tool agreed with the authored expectation. Never sufficient on its own; model agreement is not ground truth.
Written by the project as an unambiguous control; the expectation is uncontroversial and rests on the reasoning stated in the case.
Written by the project to probe a specific ambiguity; expectation rests on linguistic reasoning stated in the case.
Expectation is provisional and needs independent review.

familiarity.definition: Every checked component of the name is in routine public use in the language community (it would appear in a national top-names or surname list).
A genuine name with at least one component that is attested but uncommon in the language community.

A constructed or very unusual name in which at least one component is not found in the name references for its language community (for reference-checked cases: absent from the registered table), so a name list built from those references would not contain the combination.
The focus span is not a name candidate that has a meaningful familiarity (for example a plain common noun).

script.definition: Focus span letters are all Latin.
Focus span letters are all Hangul.
Focus span letters are all Han (hanja/kanji/hanzi).

token_class.definition: Focus span is one whitespace-delimited token.

ambiguity_level.definition: The surface form is not credibly confusable with another reading.
The surface form alone is ambiguous but the sentence context resolves it.
The context does not resolve it; both readings are defensible.

collision_classes.definition: The surface form is also an ordinary vocabulary item (Rose, Young, 하늘).
The surface form is also or is inside an organization name.
The surface form is also or is inside a place name.
The surface form is also a month, day or season (May, June).
The surface form is also or is inside a product or brand name (Ford Mustang).
The surface form is also the title of a book, song, film or similar work.
The surface form is a person's name used inside a term for a law, disease, unit, prize or similar (Ohm's law, Parkinson's disease).

context_types.definition: Focus span is at sentence start where capitalization carries no information.
Focus span is accompanied by a title or honorific.
Focus span is inside or adjacent to quotation marks.
Focus span occurs in a list or comma/slash separated sequence.
Focus span carries a possessive marker.
Korean particle is attached directly to the focus span.
Label/value or table-like text such as 'Name: ...'.
Focus span is inside parentheses or dashes.
Sentence mixes scripts around the focus span.
Text is all lowercase, ALL CAPS or headline Title Case, so capitalization carries no or misleading information.
No span in the text expects person or either: any name-like tokens are decoys.

name_features.definition: Given name plus surname (or surname plus given name).
Given name only.
Surname only.
A single name used as the whole name.
A middle name or middle initial is present.
One or more initials stand for name parts.
Jr., Sr., II, III and similar.
Hyphen inside the name.
Apostrophe inside the name (O'Neil).
Nobiliary or locative particle (de la, van der).
Name contains combining or precomposed diacritics.
Surname-comma-given order.
Korean surname followed by a given name.
Two-syllable Korean name (one-syllable surname plus one-syllable given name).
Three-syllable Korean name (the dominant pattern).
Four-syllable Korean name (two-syllable surname plus two-syllable given name, or similar).
Korean two-syllable surname such as 남궁, 황보, 선우, 독고, 제갈, 사공.
Korean surname that is uncommon.
Korean given name without surname.
Korean given name that is also an ordinary noun.
Korean name written in Latin script.
Romanized Korean name in given-then-surname order.
Korean name written or annotated in hanja.
Korean name written with internal spacing.

boundary_tags.definition: A quotation mark touches the span.
A hyphen at or inside the span edge could split the name.
An apostrophe or possessive at the span edge.
A title or honorific adjacent to the span must be excluded.
A Korean particle adjacent to the span must be excluded.
A vocative or informal suffix adjacent to the span must be excluded.
Two or more names are adjacent.
Names or particles are written without separating whitespace.
Unusual or irregular spacing around or inside the span.
Surname, Given order with a comma.
Span adjacent to parentheses or brackets.
A period belongs to an abbreviation or initial.
Script changes at the span edge.
Meaning of offsets depends on Unicode normalization.

ambiguity_kind.definition: The surface form is spelled like an ordinary word, month, day or season; only usage tells the name from the word.
The surface form is, or sits inside, a place, organization, brand, work title or eponymous term.
The mention is clear but it is open which adjacent tokens (titles, suffixes, particles, qualifiers) belong to the name span.
The mention may denote a group, family or type of person rather than one individual.
Only the surrounding format (label, column, log field, list position) says whether a token is a name.
Script, romanization, spacing or casing hides or fakes name-ness.

alternative_reading.definition: A month, day, season or other time word.
An ordinary noun, including a Korean noun that is also a given name.
An adjective, verb or other function-bearing word.
A country, city, street, river, district or other place.
A company, institution, team or other organization.
The title of a book, song, film or similar work.
A term named after a person (law, unit, prize, disease).
A family, couple, pair or plural reference.
An identifier, label, header or other field value that is not a name.
An idiom or fixed expression in which a name-shaped token is not a person.
The name of a pet, animal, vehicle or other non-human referent.
The name of a storm, festival, match or other named event.
The same person mention with a different extent.

resolving_context.definition: The verb or argument structure only fits a person (or only a non-person).
A determiner, adjective, number or quantifier selects the reading.
A title, honorific or kinship term attached to the mention.
Subject, vocative, apposition or similar position decides the reading.
A key such as 'Name:' or a column header decides the reading.
Another mention in the text (a second name, a place, an organization) decides the reading.
A Korean particle or suffix selects the reading.
A fixed phrase, idiom or collocation selects the reading.
Quotes, brackets, capitalization or layout select the reading.
Background knowledge outside the text would be needed or is relied on.
A head noun, legal-form or administrative suffix (Inc., LLP, Foundation, Street, 제지, 동) that makes the string an institution or place.
The text does not resolve the reading (genuinely ambiguous).

contrast_class.definition: A Korean particle whose form depends on whether the name ends in a consonant or a vowel (은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 과/와, 이랑/랑, 으로/로). Why: the particle is never part of the name, and a lookup that guesses the span from the surface string includes or drops the wrong syllable depending on the final sound.

A name whose last syllable is identical to a particle (지은+은, 하이+가, 도+가). Why: the particle-stripping heuristic 'drop a final 은/이/가' removes a real name syllable, so the boundary has to be decided from the whole name.
Two or more particles in sequence (에게는, 에서도, 한테서, 으로부터, 까지도, 에게만). Why: the stack is longer than any single particle and its first element can look like part of the name.
Copula and quotative endings attached to a name (입니다, 이다, 이라고, 이라는, 이란, 이며). Why: they begin with the syllable 이, which is also a frequent name syllable and the informal name suffix.
A genitive 의 or an appositive (이자, 인) after a name. Why: the following noun phrase is possessed or in apposition and the name boundary sits before 의/이자.
Honorific or role suffixes (씨, 님, 군, 양, 팀장님, 교수님, 박사), spaced or attached. Why: the suffix is excluded from the span by convention, and attached forms (김은지님) leave no whitespace cue.

A common word that begins with a syllable that is also a surname (정부, 조사, 배우), contrasted with a real name beginning with the same syllables. Why: a surname-initial heuristic fires on ordinary vocabulary.
A given name that is also an ordinary noun (가람, 한울). Why: only the predicate or particle context tells the noun from the name.

Irregular spacing: detached particles, attached titles, spaced surname and given name. Why: Korean orthography writes names without internal spaces, so spacing carries little information and tokenization assumptions break.
Names joined by middle dots, slashes or commas without spaces, or inside brackets and Korean quotation marks. Why: separators sit inside what a whitespace tokenizer calls one token.
The same person written in Hangul and Latin in one text, or a Latin name carrying a Korean particle. Why: two scripts and two mentions of one individual in one sentence.
A Hangul name touching digits, Latin letters or hanja without a space (3팀김하나, A팀의 최지훈). Why: script and digit boundaries are the only cue to the name start.
A Hangul name annotated with hanja or the reverse. Why: two mentions of one person in different scripts, with parentheses in between.

A name inside a machine-written log or key=value record (actor=..., msg="...", at ...). Why: log syntax removes sentence grammar, so capitalization, adjacency to keys and quoting are the only cues, and service, thread or class names look like surnames.
A label or key that decides whether the same value is a person (Name: Charlotte vs City: Charlotte). Why: the value alone is identical; only the key separates the readings.
A name in a pipe, tab or column layout next to cities, roles and years. Why: neighbouring cells of the same shape are not names, and a name never has surrounding prose.
A comma-delimited or inverted-order row ("Whitlow, Dana",Editor,2021). Why: commas are both delimiters and name-order markers.
Names surrounded by nested quotes, brackets, slashes, emphasis or repeated punctuation. Why: punctuation decides the span edge and must be neither absorbed nor allowed to split the name.
Names inside lightweight markup (**bold**, [link text](#anchor)). Why: markup characters sit directly against the name and are not part of it.
Less common title forms: stacked titles, Mx., Dame, Hon., titles without a period, post-nominal degrees. Why: the title-exclusion convention must hold for forms a short title list does not contain.
A name that is also an ordinary word, in a syntactic position that only a person can occupy. Why: sentence grammar, not a name list, separates the person from the word.
A product, prize, storm or eponymous term that has the shape of a person name. Why: the surface form is a name, but the referent is not a person.

familiarity_basis.definition: The label equals the frequency band of the surname component in a registered public reference table (rules in evidence/references/name-frequency-bands.json). The other components are asserted by the author to be at least as common. The check is mechanical.
The label is an authored judgment against the written criteria in docs/familiarity-and-rarity.md; no reference table was consulted for the case.
The author assembled the name (or a component of it) so that it is not an attested name; used only with familiarity novel.

case_groups.definition: Plain mentions of very common names.
Uncommon or constructed names that a routine name list may not contain.
Structural variety: middle names, initials, particles, suffixes.
Names accompanied by titles or honorifics.
Capitalization at sentence start hides or fakes name-ness.
Names that are also ordinary words.
Names that are also place names.
Names inside organization, product or brand names.
Punctuation touching or inside names.
Quotation marks and reported speech around names.
Several names next to each other.
Names in lists, labels and table-like text.
Possessives, plurals and family references.
Lowercase, ALL CAPS and headline Title Case text.
Texts with name-like tokens and no person at all.
Surname and name-length structure.
Given-name-only, vocative and informal suffix usage.
Korean particles attached to names.
Surname characters that begin or form ordinary words.
Romanized Korean names and their English collisions.
Names written across or with multiple scripts, or names next to text in another script.
Irregular spacing and separators.
Minimal pairs and honest ambiguities where the same surface form has a person and a non-person reading and the case documents what resolves it.

model_neutrality.note: Authored metadata (title, why, notes, source text) must not mention specific models, thresholds or product status. Case text itself is exempt.
